- list 3 of 3‘Our works are next to each other’: Art bridges Gaza and West Bank

While Yahya was born healthy, Ilyas was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, where he remained for nearly two weeks.

Born prematurely, Ilyas weighed just 1.4 kilogrammes (3 pounds) at birth, according to his mother. He had medical issues affecting his blood and lungs, she said, and needed specialised care in an incubator.

Rania herself was recovering from a Caesarean section when her son was taken into intensive care. For days, she could not hold him.

“When they called me to hold him, I rushed over,” she recalled. “I was in a hurry to get to him. It was such a feeling.”

As Ilyas’s condition improved and he moved from intensive care to the hospital’s neonatal care unit, Rania was able to hold him against her bare chest, introducing her to a form of care for low-birthweight newborns known as kangaroo mother care, part of a newly-launched programme at the hospital.

It involves prolonged skin-to-skin contact between a caregiver – ideally the mother – and baby, with exclusive breast milk feeding, and has been shown to have important health benefits for premature and low-birthweight babies.

“I was so happy. It was such a beautiful feeling,” Rania said.

During the session, a nurse helped Rania position Ilyas against her chest, with his skin touching hers. Rania said he remained there for about 90 minutes.

“He started breastfeeding from me, and he stayed a little longer,” she said. “I felt he was improving.”

For Rania, the contact also brought a sense of closeness after days of separation.

“The baby feels that his mother is there,” she said. “He feels safe. Honestly, it makes me very happy.”

Skin-to-skin

Kangaroo mother care involves placing a baby against a parent’s bare chest for skin-to-skin contact, alongside breastfeeding and appropriate medical care.

For premature and low-birthweight babies, it can help regulate body temperature, support breastfeeding and improve health outcomes.

World Health Organization (WHO) guidance says that kangaroo mother care has been shown to reduce neonatal mortality by 32 percent, and mortality by six months of age by 25 percent, compared with conventional care.

At Nasser Medical Complex, Khawla al-Madhoun, director of nursing at the hospital’s maternity and neonatal departments, described it as an integrated approach to newborn care that supports growth and strengthens the bond between mother and baby.

“When we place a baby on the mother’s chest, it helps the baby grow,” she said.

“We have seen babies who were unwell or underweight begin to grow faster with kangaroo care. This can help them leave the hospital sooner.”

The hospital has begun introducing kangaroo care through a pilot programme supported by WHO, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), and the UN Population Fund (UNFPA). The agencies announced the initiative at Nasser Hospital in September, but the practice is being introduced gradually in its external neonatal care unit, where babies stay with their mothers, and in maternity wards after delivery.

Al-Madhoun said the team was also preparing a dedicated room and seeking equipment to make the sessions more comfortable.

The team aims for longer periods of skin-to-skin contact – WHO recommends at least eight hours per day – although its immediate target is at least two hours, depending on each family’s circumstances.

At Nasser, the team is currently prioritising babies who are medically stable and do not require oxygen support. Nurses monitor their vital signs and assess them throughout the process.

Al-Madhoun stressed that the technique cannot replace an incubator or other treatment when a baby needs intensive care.

“It can help babies grow, gain weight and leave the hospital earlier, but some babies need other interventions, such as respiratory support,” she said. “Those babies still need the incubator and the care it provides.”

Shortage of neonatal equipment

The need for specialised newborn care comes as Gaza’s health system continues to struggle with damaged facilities, shortages of equipment and overcrowded neonatal units.

Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, Gaza had eight neonatal intensive care units with a total of 178 incubators, according to UNICEF.

By November 2024, three of those units had been destroyed by Israel, and the number of available incubators had fallen to about 54, a reduction of 70 percent. The shortage of equipment, compounded by limited supplies of fuel and electricity as a result of Israeli restrictions, put premature newborns at serious risk.

Israeli strikes have continued since an October 2025 “ceasefire”. Despite this supposed truce, and despite the delivery of some new equipment, the shortage of incubators and other equipment has persisted.

In May, UNICEF said it and its partners had supplied incubators and ventilators to hospitals in Gaza, while warning that neonatal units were still managing large numbers of fragile infants with limited equipment, space and power.

The war in Gaza has worsened living conditions for pregnant women with economic hardship, food shortages, poor nutrition and the harsh realities of displacement, including cooking over open fires and carrying water.

“These conditions have contributed to the rise in premature births and babies born with low birth weight who need specialised neonatal care,” al-Madhoun said.

Meanwhile, repeated displacement and overcrowding have placed further pressure on hospitals, including Nasser Medical Complex, which is already struggling with limited space and shortages of incubators and other essential neonatal equipment.

Newborn in a tent

Linda Abu Nasira’s baby girl is only three days old.

The infant initially developed a fever, which has since subsided, according to 23-year-old Linda.

As her daughter was being treated and breastfed, Linda was learning how to hold her against her chest under the guidance of the medical team.

The sessions were brief. Linda said she held her daughter against her chest for about 30 minutes at a time, repeating the process roughly every two hours, according to the instructions she had received.

“She is a little better than yesterday,” Linda said. “Little by little.”

Away from the hospital, Linda lives in a tent in al-Mawasi, in Khan Younis, where she is raising her two older children – aged three and two – while caring for her newborn.

She described the conditions as difficult, particularly when it comes to securing food and drinking water.

“We try to manage,” she said. “But it is not like before, or like the conditions you would expect when giving birth.”

She does not know how long the baby will need to remain under observation in the hospital’s external neonatal care unit.

“As a mother, it means a lot to me to feel that I am helping my daughter recover,” Linda said. “I hope she will recover and be discharged as soon as possible.”

articles.title: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills two, minister says
articles.summary: Yemen's information minister says the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace.
articles.preview: Two security personnel have been killed in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace, but that many others were injured. The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden".
articles.body:
Two security personnel have been killed in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say.

Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace, but that many others were injured.

The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden".

A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.

Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the Houthis' attack on Aden, calling it "cowardly" and a "continuation of their criminal behaviour".

He said the government continued to carry out its duties and vowed that it would not weaken the resolve of its forces to continue operations against the Houthis on Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines.

Earlier, the Houthis denied that they had attacked Saudi Arabia on Thursday, after the coalition said its forces had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest shrines.

The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.

On Saturday, a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, which was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis to escalate their conflict with the kingdom.

"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly told reporters, according to AFP news agency.

"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.

There was no immediate response from Iran's government. However, it has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and said it only supports them politically.

Iran's foreign minister has also said it is ready to provide "any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks" between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.

Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.

At least 1,282 people have been killed and 5,890 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.

The UN says another 201,000 people have been displaced and that there has been an alarming surge in suspected cholera cases.

articles.title: At least 5 killed in Houthi attack on Yemen’s presidential palace in Aden
articles.summary: Saudi-led coalition accuses Houthis of obtaining missile parts from regional states.
articles.preview: Saudi-led coalition accuses Houthis of obtaining missile parts from regional states. At least five people have been killed in the vicinity of the al-Maashiq presidential palace in Yemen’s port city of Aden after Houthi missile strikes. Yemeni health minister says five people were killed and 16 others injured in the Houthi missile attack that targeted the al-Maashiq Presidential Palace in Yemen’s Aden on Thursday.
articles.body:
Saudi-led coalition accuses Houthis of obtaining missile parts from regional states.

At least five people have been killed in the vicinity of the al-Maashiq presidential palace in Yemen’s port city of Aden after Houthi missile strikes.

Yemeni health minister says five people were killed and 16 others injured in the Houthi missile attack that targeted the al-Maashiq Presidential Palace in Yemen’s Aden on Thursday.

The Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said in a social media post on Thursday that Houthis had targeted the al-Maashiq presidential palace with five missiles.

The government says the prime minister and other officials are safe, but two of his bodyguards were killed in the attack.

Plumes of smoke could be seen rising from the vicinity of the palace.

Al Jazeera correspondents reported earlier on Thursday that there were explosions near the palace.

The palace is considered the headquarters and the seat of power for the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government.

Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa, said the attacks on the headquarters of the internationally recognised government are the “first of their kind” by the Houthis.

“This is an indication that the escalation is going to intensify between both sides,” Mawry said, adding that fears are now growing inside the country of “an all-out civil war” that could potentially drag in other regional powers besides Saudi Arabia.

The attack in Aden came as fighting between the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), and Saudi-backed forces intensified in Taiz, which is effectively under siege by the Houthis.

Controlling Taiz, Yemen’s third city and the broader Taiz governorate, in the southwest of the country would ensure control over the critical Bab al-Mandeb strait for either side.

Forces allied with the Yemeni government said they are repelling a Houthi attack on Dhubab airport.

The pro-government Homeland Shield Force said in a statement that they are, along with the Southern Giants Brigades, securing the airport in the coastal city of Dhubab in Taiz governorate.

Aid agencies say the escalating violence in Taiz is pushing the healthcare system towards breaking point.

On Sunday, the Ministry of Public Health warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” there.

Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition says Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has come under at least 20 Houthi attacks over the past 11 days with dozens of other airports, oil facilities and ports also targeted.

Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the alliance, released footage showing strikes on the main airport with passengers seen fleeing for safety, during a news conference in the Saudi capital,

The coalition says the Houthi attacks have killed 17 people and injured more than 300.

Al-Maliki also accused the Houthis of obtaining ballistic missiles from other countries in the region.

Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, said the Saudi-led coalition’s news conference was intended as a response “to some of the, perhaps, military and security failures”.

“There’s kind of an image problem there because this is maybe affecting the perception of Saudi deterrence, the fact that missiles are getting through,” he told Al Jazeera.

Elmasry said the Houthis also have an image crisis, with the global community viewing their actions as “reprehensible, in particular these targeting civilian infrastructure”.

articles.title: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
articles.summary: Ukraine's president says a pause on striking energy sites is over following fresh Russian attacks.
articles.preview: Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume. Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days while Russia continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times, external. Russian President Vladimir Putin said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied - but there had been no "significant damage".
articles.body:
Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume.

Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days while Russia continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times, external.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied - but there had been no "significant damage".

Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks but Ukrainian defence sources later told the BBC some functionality on Starlink satellite services had resumed.

They said "operation while on the move", part of Starlink's military service Starshield, had been restored, although it remains unclear whether restrictions on the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection have been fully lifted.

Officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances" behind the move, the sources added.

In a separate development, seven people are missing after a drone attack set a chemical tanker on fire off Romania, according to naval officials. Moscow said it had hit two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port, without naming them.

The Kremlin said Kyiv had "attempted a large-scale attack" on a refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.

According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.

Zelensky said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.

He previously said he would agree to the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.

But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal.

Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.

European leaders have rallied around the Ukrainian president. Italy's Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that the US restricting its intelligence-sharing with Kyiv would be a "complete mistake".

"Because it is a fundamental form of support. This means denying a country any chance of defending itself."

He added: "Peace will be achieved when Putin will be convinced that there is a stalemate... that he cannot advance anymore. But if he sees a weakness on the Ukrainian front, if the United States takes its resources away, then Putin will think he can win, and so he will continue the war."

Zelensky met Nato chief Mark Rutte as a two-day summit of European leaders began in Brussels on Thursday. The head of the military alliance said they had discussed "the importance of implementing an energy ceasefire as well as Nato allies' continuous support for Ukraine".

Zelensky told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".

Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.

There were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame for the sudden Starlink restrictions on Tuesday evening, but owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this and suggested it was the Trump administration's doing.

"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.

Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing. Starlink's sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US defence department contract. The BBC has approached the US authorities for comment.

Zelensky spoke to the FT during a visit to London on Wednesday which also included a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street - who announced the UK would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Kyiv.

The Ukrainian president told the newspaper he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles.

Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles.

Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Putin.

He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week: "We didn't destroy any relationship."

Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal.

Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just.

But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.

That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing.

Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."

With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.

Local officials report at least 13 people were killed across Ukraine on Wednesday in what Zelensky called a "constant", large-scale Russian attack. He said more than 850 drones had been launched at dozens of cities and communities.

At least three people were killed in the central region of Kirovohrad as it suffered its largest attack since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, officials there said, with nearly 360 drones launched during a 10-hour barrage. Deaths were also reported in Donetsk, Kherson and Volyn.

"It is clear that Russia deliberately escalated these attacks, taking advantage of the easing of sanctions and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelensky wrote on social media.

articles.title: ¿Sobran kilos o falta testosterona? Uno de cada cuatro soldados estadounidenses puede tener niveles bajos de esta hormona
articles.summary: El cribado masivo impulsado por Trump para su “Departamento de Guerra de alta testosterona” se arriesga a encontrar niveles muy bajos, según un estudio
articles.preview: Las palabras son importantes. A veces describen una realidad. Otras, pretenden modificarla. articles.body:
Tra l’11 e il 13 ottobre cinquecento supermercati della grande distribuzione francese hanno subìto un attacco hacker agli impianti di refrigerazione. Le apparecchiature, tutte prodotte dall’azienda danese Danfoss, sono state sabotate e le temperature portate fino a 50 gradi: la rottura della catena del freddo ha deteriorato irrimediabilmente tonnellate di prodotti, che sono stati buttati. I sistemi di congelamento sono stati manomessi a distanza e secondo la Danfoss, scrive La Dépêche, si trattava di dispositivi vecchi, prossimi alla fine del loro ciclo vitale e privi degli aggiornamenti di sicurezza. Diverse vulnerabilità erano già state documentate da parte dei controllori dell’azienda, tra cui falle nell’autenticazione e nell’inserimento dei comandi. L’identità dei responsabili, le loro motivazioni e l’eventuale coordinamento sono ancora ignoti. Ma attacchi hacker alla grande distribuzione sono stati denunciati negli stessi giorni nei Paesi Bassi, dove sono stati messi fuori uso lo shopping online e i cartellini elettronici di alcuni supermercati, e in Belgio, dove sono stati segnalati problemi al sistema informatico. ◆

articles.title: Un premio Nobel in difesa della giustizia

articles.body:
diritto internazionale

Anche quest’anno Donald Trump ha visto il premio Nobel per la pace sfuggirgli di mano. E, dalla sua prospettiva, il peggio è che gliel’ha soffiato Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, 85 anni, che rappresenta tutto ciò che lui respinge. Dopo una lunga carriera come avvocata e giudice in Sudafrica, suo paese d’origine, e successivamente ai vertici delle istituzioni giudiziarie internazionali, la magistrata simboleggia la contrapposizione tra il diritto internazionale e il ricorso alla forza.

Il 9 ottobre il comitato norvegese per il Nobel ha reso omaggio a una donna che, “con coraggio e integrità eccezionali, ha aperto la strada a un ordinamento giuridico più solido”. È stata premiata per “l’impegno a favore della pace e del diritto internazionale”, in un momento storico in cui “i giudici e le istituzioni del diritto internazionale sono sotto attacco”.

In un comunicato il segretario generale delle Nazioni Unite, António Guterres, si è rallegrato del riconoscimento a “una paladina del diritto internazionale e dei diritti umani, e una voce decisa e indipendente in alcuni dei procedimenti giudiziari internazionali più importanti della nostra storia”.

“Se applaudite ancora un po’, dividerò il premio con Trump!”, ha scherzato Pillay nel ricevere la notizia. Al momento dell’annuncio “stava partecipando a una conferenza nell’aula 600 del tribunale di Norimberga”, la stessa dove ottant’anni prima erano stati processati i gerarchi nazisti dopo la seconda guerra mondiale, racconta Cécile Aptel, che si trovava con lei. Aptel era consigliera di Pillay quando guidava l’Alto commissariato delle Nazioni Unite per i diritti umani (2008-2014). “Non sapeva neanche di essere candidata”, dice commentando il premio.

Come si vede in un video sui social media, in un discorso improvvisato Pillay ha ricordato: “L’ultima cosa che ho fatto è stato il rapporto su Gaza in cui si dice che quello che sta avvenendo è un genocidio”. Il 16 settembre 2025 una commissione d’inchiesta, da lei presieduta, dell’Alto commissariato delle Nazioni Unite per i diritti umani aveva presentato un rapporto esplosivo. “È chiaro”, aveva detto la magistrata, “che esiste un’intenzione di distruggere i palestinesi di Gaza attraverso atti che corrispondono ai criteri stabiliti dalla Convenzione” sul genocidio.

Se esistesse “un premio per le menzogne e l’odio”, sarebbe lei a vincerlo, ha fatto sapere il 9 ottobre il ministero degli esteri israeliano, secondo cui “il comitato del Nobel ha premiato la più grande menzogna del ventunesimo secolo. Joseph Goebbels (1897-1945) starà sicuramente applaudendo dall’inferno”. Il primo ministro israeliano, Benjamin Netanyahu, ha definito Pillay “fanatica”, aggiungendo che “demonizza gli ebrei”.

Di tutt’altro tenore la reazione del ministero degli esteri palestinese, che ha accolto con favore la scelta: “Nel corso della sua brillante carriera, ha cercato la verità e difeso i diritti degli oppressi in Sudafrica e in tutto il mondo, compresa la Palestina, con integrità, coraggio e onore”.

Arrivano le sanzioni

Mentre da Mosca a Washington, da Tel Aviv a Teheran, da Al Fashir, in Sudan, a Goma, nell’est della Repubblica Democratica del Congo, il diritto internazionale è calpestato e le sue istituzioni subiscono numerosi attacchi, il Nobel rappresenta tutto quello che l’amministrazione Trump e il governo Netanyahu vorrebbero “smantellare”. Figura molto nota in questo ambiente, Pillay rivendica il suo essere un’“universalista”.

Dall’inizio del 2025 tredici giudici e procuratori della Corte penale internazionale (Cpi) sono stati colpiti dalle sanzioni statunitensi. Poche ore dopo l’annuncio del Nobel, il segretario di stato Marco Rubio ha annunciato che Washington aveva deciso nuove sanzioni direttamente contro la Cpi, il tribunale in cui Pillay ha prestato servizio come giudice dal 2003 al 2008. È la prima volta che succede, prima era stati sanzionati solo i singoli giudici.

Da mesi l’amministrazione Trump chiede l’annullamento dei mandati d’arresto emessi dalla Cpi nel novembre 2024 nei confronti di Netanyahu e del suo ex ministro della difesa, Yoav Gallant.

E Washington non è da sola in questo attacco alla Cpi: l’8 ottobre la Russia ha chiesto l’estradizione di nove giudici della corte e dell’ex procuratore Karim Khan. Alla fine del dicembre 2025 erano stati condannati in contumacia da un tribunale di Mosca a pene comprese fra i tre e i quindici anni di reclusione, di cui sei anni in una colonia penale per Khan.

Dall’apartheid al Ruanda

L’impegno di Navanethem Pillay è emerso fin dall’inizio della sua carriera professionale. “Ha fatto un percorso straordinario dimostrando un coraggio eccezionale”, dice Aptel. “Era una giovane povera di una famiglia indiana della provincia del KwaZulu-Natal, diventata avvocata nel Sudafrica dell’apartheid e arrivata a presiedere una commissione d’inchiesta su una questione estremamente delicata. Oggi dedica il suo premio alle vittime e ai sopravvissuti”.

Nata nel 1941 a Durban, in una famiglia tamil, Pillay riuscì a frequentare l’università grazie al sostegno della comunità indiana, che contribuì a pagarle gli studi. Ai tempi dell’apartheid gli indiani erano considerati appena un gradino sopra i neri e i coloured, ma erano comunque sottoposti al rigido regime di “sviluppo separato” imposto dai nazionalisti afrikaner al potere. Luoghi di residenza, professioni, spostamenti, accesso alle spiagge, ai ristoranti e ai trasporti: tutto era regolamentato.

Pillay s’inserisce anche nella tradizione di grandi giuristi che hanno portato avanti la lotta contro l’apartheid, come Nelson Mandela. Nel 1952 lui e Oliver Tambo furono i primi sudafricani neri ad aprire uno studio legale.

Dopo la laurea, nel 1965, aprì il suo studio da avvocata. “Non avevo scelta”, ha raccontato alla Bbc nel 2008. “Nessuno voleva assumermi. Dicevano che era impensabile che i dipendenti bianchi ricevessero ordini da una persona non bianca”. In quegli anni difese gli attivisti antiapartheid arrestati dal governo, denunciò le conseguenze della tortura e dell’isolamento dei prigionieri politici e ottenne condizioni migliori per quelli che erano reclusi a Robben Island, tra cui Nelson Mandela. Dopo l’avvento della democrazia e l’elezione di Mandela a presidente nel 1994, diventò la prima donna non bianca a far parte dell’alta corte del Sudafrica.

Nel 1996 Pillay fu nominata al Tribunale penale internazionale per il Ruanda, istituito dalle Nazioni Unite per giudicare i crimini commessi durante il genocidio dei tutsi, che nel 1994 aveva causato circa un milione di morti. Fu fra i tre magistrati che il 2 settembre 1998 pronunciarono la prima condanna per genocidio emessa da un tribunale internazionale nei confronti di Jean-Paul Akayesu, che all’epoca del genocidio era sindaco di Taba, un comune del Ruanda centrale. Successivamente Pillay ha presieduto per quattro anni il tribunale internazionale sul Ruanda. Oggi è giudice in un procedimento avviato dal Gambia davanti alla Corte internazionale di giustizia (Cig), il massimo organo giudiziario dell’Onu, contro la Birmania, accusata di violare la Convenzione sul genocidio prendendo di mira la minoranza rohingya.

L’assegnazione del premio Nobel per la pace a questa autorevole giudice internazionale è stata accolta con favore dal presidente sudafricano Cyril Ramaphosa, il cui paese è stato ripetutamente attaccato dall’amministrazione Trump da quando, nel dicembre 2023, ha presentato un ricorso contro Israele davanti alla Cig, accusandolo di violare la Convenzione sul genocidio. “Il riconoscimento che le viene conferito ci ricorda la necessità di costruire una società in cui ognuno, indipendentemente dalla sua condizione, possa sviluppare le proprie capacità e contribuire pienamente alla vita del nostro paese e del mondo”, ha detto Ramaphosa. ◆ gim

articles.title: Gli Stati Uniti cambiano strategia sull’Ucraina

articles.body:
Il 9 ottobre, quando gli inviati degli Stati Uniti Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner hanno comunicato la decisione di Donald Trump di cancellare le sanzioni sulle esportazioni di gasolio russo, i componenti della delegazione ucraina stentavano a crederci.

I negoziatori di Kiev, arrivati negli Stati Uniti per discutere un possibile cessate il fuoco energetico con la Russia, sono stati presi alla sprovvista da una scelta che potrebbe garantire a Mosca le risorse per continuare a finanziare la guerra, compromettendo la posizione di Kiev nella trattativa con il Cremlino. “Non c’era solo la nostra delegazione, ma anche quella europea”, ha raccontato un funzionario ucraino. “E ce ne stavamo tutti seduti lì come degli imbecilli”.

Dopo aver chiesto all’Ucraina di fermare gli attacchi contro le infrastrutture energetiche russe, Washington ha regalato a Mosca anche un insperato aiuto economico. Il tutto mentre Trump deve affrontare le conseguenze della guerra contro l’Iran. “È stato lui a trascinare il mondo in questa guerra senza via d’uscita. E ora ci tradisce perché ha bisogno di una boccata d’ossigeno prima delle elezioni di metà mandato”, ha detto il funzionario ucraino.

Il Kyiv Independent ha parlato con diverse fonti vicine alla trattativa. Tutte hanno chiesto di mantenere l’anonimato.

Per il governo ucraino la vera questione è perché Kiev dovrebbe rinunciare a uno strumento per fare pressione su Mosca, senza che anche i russi siano obbligati a sospendere gli attacchi.

Il presidente Volodymyr Zelenskyj aveva inviato una delegazione negli Stati Uniti per un incontro in cui si doveva discutere l’ipotesi di un cessate il fuoco energetico e un accordo separato per mettere fine agli attacchi sul mar Nero. La trattativa, però, è saltata quando Trump – dopo una telefonata con il presidente russo Vladimir Putin – ha annunciato che Mosca fornirà milioni di tonnellate di diesel agli Stati Uniti e al mercato globale.

L’Ucraina non era stata informata in anticipo della decisione. Anche se Zelenskyj ha ammesso pubblicamente che Washington stava valutando la possibilità di trovare un’intesa con Mosca, i funzionari ucraini raccontano di non aver ricevuto nessuna comunicazione prima dell’annuncio del 9 ottobre.

Per la delegazione di Kiev la notizia alimenta il dubbio che gli Stati Uniti avessero già stabilito i termini dell’accordo con Mosca, mentre i funzionari ucraini ed europei stavano ancora cercando di negoziare una tregua energetica. “È sembrata una trappola”, sottolinea il funzionario ucraino. In effetti, la tempistica della decisione statunitense giustifica questi sospetti.

Su istruzioni di Trump, il dipartimento del tesoro degli Stati Uniti ha quindi annunciato che l’Ufficio di controllo dei beni stranieri avrebbe “immediatamente emesso una licenza temporanea e generale per consentire l’immissione del gasolio russo nel mercato globale”.

Un altro funzionario ucraino ritiene che la data del 7 aprile come scadenza dell’attuale deroga sia un indizio del fatto che Washington aveva pianificato la nuova misura seguendo un programma preciso: “Hanno deciso che le sanzioni saranno cancellate fino al 7 aprile 2027, e queste misure vanno di sei mesi in sei mesi. Quindi evidentemente avevano preparato tutto per il 7 ottobre, che è il giorno del compleanno di Putin. Era un regalo per il presidente russo”.

◆ Il 9 ottobre 2026 Donald Trump ha annunciato la sospensione di alcune sanzioni statunitensi sul gasolio russo, autorizzandone la vendita, il trasporto e l’importazione, anche negli Stati Uniti, fino al 7 aprile 2027. Due giorni dopo ha annunciato un cessate il fuoco immediato tra Russia e Ucraina limitato alle infrastrutture energetiche. Ma l’accordo non era stato negoziato con le parti. Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelenskyj si è detto disponibile a rispettarlo, a patto che anche Mosca interrompa gli attacchi. Il Cremlino ha fatto sapere di non essere interessato e ha subito lanciato un attacco su sei infrastrutture energetiche ucraine. Washington ha anche minacciato di sospendere le forniture militari e la condivisione dell’intelligence se Kiev continuerà a colpire le raffinerie russe. Nei giorni seguenti l’esercito russo è tornato a bombardare l’Ucraina. Nelle notti tra il 12 e il 14 ottobre gli attacchi su Kiev e altre città del paese hanno fatto almeno 19 morti e più di cento feriti. Il governo ucraino ha dichiarato di non aver ricevuto dagli alleati informazioni preventive sul lancio dei missili russi. L’episodio sembra confermare il timore che Washington abbia ridotto la condivisione di informazioni con Kiev, ma Trump ha affermato che la collaborazione sull’intelligence è ancora in vigore. La settimana precedente, tra l’8 e il 10 ottobre, i bombardamenti russi avevano provocato più di sessanta morti, tra cui 35 persone uccise nell’attacco a due minibus a Kramatorsk. L’11 ottobre i droni ucraini hanno invece colpito un data center dell’azienda tecnologica russa Yandex. Reuters

L’ombra dell’Iran

In ogni modo, le tensioni tra Stati Uniti e Ucraina stavano montando da settimane. Trump aveva già intimato al presidente ucraino di fermare i bombardamenti sulle infrastrutture energetiche russe. “Zelenskyj deve fare una sola cosa: smettere di attaccare il diesel in Russia”, aveva detto il 13 settembre.

Ma Kiev aveva respinto la proposta di interrompere le incursioni unilateralmente. Secondo i funzionari ucraini, Zelenskyj aveva chiarito più volte che qualsiasi cessate il fuoco energetico doveva riguardare entrambe le parti, e che quindi anche Mosca doveva interrompere gli attacchi.

Per Kiev questo è un punto fondamentale: le offensive ucraine contro raffinerie, terminali petroliferi e altre infrastrutture energetiche hanno l’obiettivo di bloccare uno dei motori della macchina bellica del Cremlino. La Russia, invece, prende di mira centrali elettriche e sottostazioni per privare i civili di corrente e riscaldamento. Un cessate il fuoco che metta fine solo agli attacchi ucraini non frenerebbe le offensive russe contro l’Ucraina, ma proteggerebbe le strutture che le alimentano.

I funzionari ucraini hanno raccontato che i negoziatori statunitensi hanno presentato l’accordo in una luce diversa, puntando il dito contro Zelenskyj e attribuendo l’impasse attuale al suo rifiuto di fermare gli attacchi. Secondo una persona presente all’incontro, agli ucraini è stato inoltre fatto presente che Washington intende smettere di condividere le informazioni dell’intelligence con Kiev.

“A questo punto spero che gli americani non consegnino ai russi i Patriot (sistemi di difesa aerea) per proteggere le loro raffinerie…”, ha commentato sarcasticamente uno di loro.

Queste parole riassumono una paura assolutamente reale a Kiev. Già in passato Washington aveva aiutato Mosca a proteggere le infrastrutture che finanziano la guerra, spingendo nello stesso tempo l’Ucraina a rinunciare ai mezzi per contrattaccare.

Per Kiev, il punto è sempre lo stesso: una tregua energetica può funzionare solo se entrambi i governi accettano le stesse restrizioni. “Ma con la sua ultima mossa Trump ha sepolto ogni possibilità di un cessate il fuoco. È stata un’idiozia”, ha detto un altro funzionario ucraino, suggerendo che Washington sta cercando di privare Kiev della sua carta principale al tavolo dei negoziati.

Intanto la situazione sul terreno dimostra che la mossa di Washington non ha cambiato granché. Poche ore dopo l’annuncio di Trump i droni ucraini hanno colpito un terminale russo per il carico del petrolio a Rostov sul Don, una struttura che lavora per le esportazioni e fornisce carburante all’esercito. Il 10 ottobre, invece, la Russia ha lanciato un attacco con droni e missili su Kiev, prendendo di mira gli impianti energetici.

Nessuno dei due schieramenti, insomma, ha smesso di colpire le infrastrutture energetiche nemiche: l’annuncio statunitense evidentemente non ha ridotto la distanza tra Mosca e Kiev.

Zelenskyj ha commentato la decisione di Trump in un messaggio vocale inviato ai giornalisti il 9 ottobre, sottolineando che l’esportazione di diesel porterà a Mosca nuove risorse per finanziare la guerra. “Proprio mentre si parla di pace, gli Stati Uniti autorizzano la Russia a esportare il suo gasolio. Questo favorisce Putin e gli consente di continuare a combattere”, ha detto, prima di mettere in dubbio l’utilità di inviare delegazioni di funzionari in incontri del genere. “I nostri negoziatori sono stati usati come copertura. È un atteggiamento poco onesto. Non è così che si comportano gli alleati”.

Gli Stati Uniti hanno anche chiesto all’Ucraina di fare concessioni territoriali, mentre Mosca continuava ad attaccare le città e le infrastrutture del paese.

Per un funzionario ucraino la spiegazione è chiara: Trump sta cercando di scaricare la responsabilità dei suoi fallimenti in politica estera. “Chiaramente non vuole ammettere”, ha detto, “che è stata la sua guerra contro l’Iran a causare così tanti problemi agli statunitensi”. ◆ as

articles.title: La storia del crollo dei bot russi dopo gli attacchi ucraini a Yandex è priva di riscontri
articles.summary: Si è molto diffusa online in questi giorni, ma analisi indipendenti hanno mostrato che non esistono dati per confermarla
articles.preview: Altri osservatori, basandosi su proprie analisi, hanno invece sostenuto che, dopo l’attacco ai server russi di Yandex, i contenuti legati alle campagna di disinformazione russa che prendono di mira tematiche come le prossime elezioni presidenziali francesi avrebbero ottenuto su X solo poche decine di migliaia di visualizzazioni. articles.body:
Altri osservatori, basandosi su proprie analisi, hanno invece sostenuto che, dopo l’attacco ai server russi di Yandex, i contenuti legati alle campagna di disinformazione russa che prendono di mira tematiche come le prossime elezioni presidenziali francesi avrebbero ottenuto su X solo poche decine di migliaia di visualizzazioni. A settembre, prima dei droni ucraini, questi contenuti ne avrebbero ottenute milioni.

Verifiche indipendenti e molti esperti di disinformazione hanno spiegato tuttavia che non esistono ad oggi dati affidabili e verificabili che dimostrino che ci sia stato un calo significativo dell’attività di influenza russa online dopo l’attacco ucraino alle infrastrutture di Yandex.

Cosa dicono le analisi e le indagini indipendenti

Da più parti si è provato subito a fare chiarezza su come andassero interpretati i grafici utilizzati come prova. L’istituto di monitoraggio dei media polacco Emocje w slacieci ha chiarito innanzitutto un concetto, la cui scarsa conoscenza ha favorito il diffondersi di questa narrazione: un bot non è necessariamente un account falso che diffonde propaganda del Cremlino sui social media. Inoltre, nel caso dell’attacco ai server di Yandex, a essere rilevato era stato il crollo dell’attività dei cosiddetti web crawler, ossia i programmi automatici impiegati da ogni motore di ricerca, incluso quello russo di Yandex, per esplorare il web e per indicizzarne i contenuti. La stessa Cloudflare, riporta la BBC, ha chiarito che i suoi dati includono tutte le richieste Internet automatizzate ai siti web ospitati sulla sua rete, compresi i bot che scansionano i siti web alla ricerca di informazioni. L’azienda statunitense ha inoltre specificato all’emittente pubblica che il calo mostrato nel grafico «non è necessariamente dovuto al comportamento dei bot sulle piattaforme dei social media».

Il secondo grafico, invece, quello che avrebbe mostrato il crollo delle attività online riguardanti AfD dopo gli attacchi ucraini, risulta essere privo di qualsiasi riscontro. Il grafico in questione infatti, oltre a non aver alcuna fonte indicata sulla provenienza dei dati e a non risultare chiaro nella dicitura “attività giornaliera”, risulta essere stato pubblicato su Threads per la prima volta l’11 ottobre. Tuttavia, nell’asse orizzontale del diagramma i dati arrivano fino al “15 ottobre”, quindi una data futura.

Agli esperti di disinformazione l’idea che un semplice attacco di questo tipo potesse portare a un crollo delle operazioni di influenza russa è suonata subito molto semplicistica: parlando col Guardian, Ned Mendez, responsabile della ricerca dell’organizzazione Alliance4Europe che si batte contro la disinformazione, ha spiegato che per evitare di essere segnalate come sospette dalle piattaforme, le bot farm operano con modalità che ne favoriscono la distribuzione e la resilienza, per esempio attraverso connessioni residenziali e phone farm. «Non possiamo semplicemente cancellare i bot a forza di bombe, per quanto l’idea possa sembrare allettante», ha dichiarato Mendez.

Vari istituti che analizzano la disinformazione online hanno invece segnalato che, dal canto loro, non era stata individuata nessuna correlazione tra l’attacco ai data center di Yandex e un crollo del traffico di certi account. Come riportato dalla testata tedesca Capital, sia l’Istituto di ricerca Cemas che il think tank Polisphere – entrambi impegnati nell’analisi di disinformazione e nel monitoraggio social di account tedeschi attribuibili ad attori della disinformazione, sostenitori dell’AfD e gruppi di diffusori filoruss – non si sono registrati cali statisticamente significativi dell’attività nei Paesi di lingua tedesca. Sono state dello stesso tenore le affermazioni di altri analisti e del gruppo BotBlocker, specializzato nell’analisi di troll farm russe presenti sulle piattaforme social.

Quando le affermazioni categoriche delle prime ore sono state messe in discussione, non trovando conferme indipendenti, alcuni dei profili che più avevano contribuito a diffondere questa narrazione sono intervenuti di nuovo per scusarsi o ridimensionare la propria posizione iniziale. L’analista militare polacco Jaroslav Wolski che aveva postato il grafico infondato su AfD ha cancellato il tweet e scritto un secondo post sull’argomento: «Purtroppo il mio post contenente disinformazione ha raggiunto milioni di visualizzazioni, e per questo desidero scusarmi ancora una volta con tutti i lettori. Naturalmente mi assumo la piena responsabilità di ciò che ho fatto e, in modo semplice e umano, mi vergogno di avervi disinformato. Chiedo scusa anche agli oppositori che avevo contestato e che sono stati i primi a farmi notare che mi sbagliavo».

Mentre in risposta a una richiesta di informazioni da parte di ZDFheute, l’eurodeputato ceco Zdechovský ha ammesso di non possedere attualmente dati verificabili in modo indipendente che provino in modo definitivo un collegamento tra gli attacchi e un calo dell’attività delle reti di disinformazione russe. «Non ho mai affermato che tale collegamento sia stato definitivamente dimostrato», ha aggiunto.

L’ufficio di Zelensky ha dichiarato alla BBC che il presidente ucraino si riferiva «all’atmosfera sui social media» piuttosto che a una diminuzione dell’attività dei bot, aggiungendo di aver ricevuto «segnalazioni di un minor numero di commenti provocatori e di incitamento all’odio» da parte di molti utenti dei social media.

Le conseguenze provate degli attacchi ucraini

Come abbiamo visto, quindi, non ci sono prove che permettano di concludere che gli attacchi ai data center di Yandex abbiano avuto un impatto sulle operazioni di influenza della Russia. Ma questo non significa che non ci siano state conseguenze in Russia.

Come scrive Meduza – media russo indipendente con sede in Lettonia, bloccato in Russia perché considerato «organizzazione indesiderabile» – i droni ucraini hanno creato interruzioni diffuse su tutta la rete internet russa, bloccando temporaneamente i servizi di Yandex, tra cui Yandex Go, Yandex Eats e Yandex Pay, utilizzati in gran numero di russi. Inoltre, molti altri siti web e servizi sono andati offline, tra cui quelli di importanti banche, rivenditori, marketplace online, piattaforme di annunci classificati, siti web e app di notizie e molto altro. Questo perché queste aziende utilizzavano l’infrastruttura di Yandex per archiviare i propri dati. I russi, inoltre, continua Meduza, hanno perso l’accesso a una serie di servizi di uso quotidiano, come chiamare un taxi, effettuare pagamenti, ordinare consegne, controllare la posta elettronica. Fino al 13 ottobre, la stessa Yandex aveva comunicato ai propri utenti di star continuando a lavorare per ripristinare il funzionamento completo delle proprie attività.

Il Financial Times riporta che i disagi si sono estesi anche ai paesi confinanti con la Russia, con interruzioni dei servizi di posta elettronica, Yandex Pay e siti web che utilizzano l’infrastruttura dell’azienda russa in Kazakistan, Uzbekistan e Bielorussia. Nel 2024 Yandex era stata venduta forzatamente a investitori legati al presidente russo Vladimir Putin. All’epoca il vicepresidente della commissione parlamentare russa sull’informazione, Anton Gorelkin, aveva detto che «Yandex è più di un’azienda, è una risorsa per l’intera società russa».

Non possiamo accettare che l'Italia versi di più al bilancio europeo e, allo stesso tempo riceva di meno. è una semplice questione di equità". "Più sicurezza non significa meno ospedali" "Ricordo che la maggiore flessibilità per difesa e sicurezza significa essenzialmente risorse aggiuntive rispetto a quelle consentite dai parametri europei. Chi racconta che più sicurezza significa meno ospedali, risorse distratte dai servizi essenziali da un governo di guerrafondai, mente sapendo di farlo", ha proseguito Meloni, nell'aula del Senato, nel corso delle comunicazioni in vista della riunione del Consiglio europeo di domani e dopodomani. E allora non c'era neanche la guerra in Ucraina".

articles.title: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access
articles.summary: METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the frontier AI model maker has given up the right to block them.
articles.preview: Anthropic is giving employee-level access to six researchers from METR, a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, to independently assess Anthropic’s models, safety practices, and risk management, the company said in a blog post on Thursday. The arrangement comes at a time where incidents of AI agents acting outside their instructions have been disclosed every week or two since late August. The incidents have sharpened calls for independent checks on AI companies.
articles.body:
Anthropic is giving employee-level access to six researchers from METR, a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, to independently assess Anthropic’s models, safety practices, and risk management, the company said in a blog post on Thursday.

The arrangement comes at a time where incidents of AI agents acting outside their instructions have been disclosed every week or two since late August. The incidents have sharpened calls for independent checks on AI companies.

“We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making,” Anthropic said in the blog post. “We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.”

Under the new arrangement, the METR team has Anthropic-issued company laptops, office space, and access to internal tools roughly on par with what Anthropic’s own risk assessment teams use. “Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk” the company said.

Anthropic compared the arrangement to banking, similar to how regulators place resident examiners inside the largest banks.

METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the company has given up the right to block them.

“Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, pre-defined categories,” the company said, such as customer data, anything attorney-client privileged, or relating to information about its model architectures. “METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information” Anthropic added.

METR is the only evaluator so far at the top of a three-tier system Anthropic is building. Evaluators in the bottom tier, like biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio, run narrow reviews and require Anthropic’s approval to publish. The middle tier gets more information and can publish without approval, while the top tier adds METR’s employee-level access.

Thursday’s announcement makes good on a promise Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made in a September essay, where he proposed embedding outside evaluators inside AI labs as a first step toward slowing the technology’s development. OpenAI quickly pledged the same, and both companies, along with Google, Meta, Nvidia, and xAI, have since signed a White House accord committing to independent review.

articles.title: Volvo makes a bigger bet on Nvidia for hands-free automated driving
articles.summary: Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia that will extend beyond its battery electric vehicles.
articles.preview: Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. The companies announced on Thursday that Volvo will use three pieces of Nvidia hardware and software in its future vehicles to provide an automated driving system that can navigate urban streets and highways. Under the expanded partnership, Volvo will combine its vehicle safety systems and engineering with Nvidia’s Hyperion sensor and compute architecture, Alpamayo driving software stack, and Halos safety evaluation layer.
articles.body:
Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. The companies announced on Thursday that Volvo will use three pieces of Nvidia hardware and software in its future vehicles to provide an automated driving system that can navigate urban streets and highways.

Under the expanded partnership, Volvo will combine its vehicle safety systems and engineering with Nvidia’s Hyperion sensor and compute architecture, Alpamayo driving software stack, and Halos safety evaluation layer.

The Alpamayo stack is redundant and diverse, according to Ali Kani, who heads up Nvidia’s automotive division. It combines Alpamayo, a family of AI models, datasets, and simulation and development tools used to build autonomous-driving software, with classical software that uses machine learning and camera and radar perception, he said.

“The point is we run these two stacks at the same time, and we have multimodal sensors in our philosophy because it’s a safer product that way,” Kani said, adding that the open source Alpamayo software has now been downloaded by more than 650,000 developers.

Volvo didn’t reveal the value of the partnership or which vehicle model would be the first to use this new Nvidia tech stack. But Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo’s head of software development, hinted at the scale of the deal and how it represents the automaker’s evolution toward developing a full-tech stack designed for its electric vehicles as well as its plug-in hybrids and gas-powered vehicles.

“Automakers used to be very much like car-line-based development and working with various suppliers, etc. and we have completely changed and migrated into being a full-tech stack company,” Bakkenes said, adding that Volvo will start this partnership with a brand new vehicle that “will come in the not-too-near future.”

He said the first vehicle with this new Nvidia tech stack will debut within the decade, and “then of course the technology can go beyond that.”

While Volvo’s relationship with Nvidia isn’t new, the expanded partnership represents the automaker’s effort to bring the latest automated driving software to all of its vehicles — not just its EVs.

All of Volvo’s battery-electric vehicles use Nvidia’s Orin computer chip, which processes information from cameras, radar, and other sensors to help a vehicle understand its surroundings and make driving decisions.

“What we’re going to do in the future is actually standardize more on Hyperion — also from a sensor set perspective — to really open up the stack for the wider partnership with Nvidia,” Bakkenes said.

articles.body:
Volvo plans to launch hands-free, point-to-point driving by 2030, powered by Nvidia’s latest AI technology. The Chinese-owned, Swedish-designed automaker said Thursday it would use Nvidia’s autonomous driving stack to power a new partially automated driving system similar to Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised).

The system will be similar to Tesla’s Full Self-Driving in that it will enable hands-free, point-to-point partially automated driving on local roads.

Volvo says the new point-to-point system will be Level 2++, meaning it can handle complex urban environments, including traffic lights, stop signs, and unprotected left turns without explicit driver control. In addition to Tesla’s FSD, it will also resemble the Nvidia-powered system that Mercedes-Benz recently rolled out for the all-new CLA sedan, said Ali Kani, VP and general manager of the automotive team at Nvidia, in an interview with The Verge.

Volvo will use Nvidia’s Hyperion platform, which includes the chipmaker’s high-powered silicon, as well as additional sensors mounted around the vehicle so the car can see and perceive its surroundings. The automaker will also utilize Nvidia’s Alpamayo software, which uses “reasoning” models to make sense of complex road conditions and plan where to steer, brake, or accelerate. The setup will not include lidar, though it could include the laser sensor if Volvo decides to add it in the future.

By expanding its preexisting partnership with Volvo, the automaker is trying to correct some of its failed automated driving projects of the past. The automaker had to effectively sideline its Ride Pilot Level 3 unsupervised autonomous driving system in the US after failing to obtain regulatory approval. Volvo also planned to add lidar sensors to some of its models, but that plan fell away after its supplier Luminar went bankrupt.

Volvo is also bringing its own reputation for safety to the table. The automaker wants to combine its safety expertise with Nvidia’s technology to improve the overall system, including contributing its proprietary driver-understanding systems, which analyze driver behavior in considerably greater detail than a basic driver monitoring system, said Alwin Bakkenes, head of global software engineering at Volvo Cars.

“Our brand Volvo is synonymous with safety, and safety is synonymous with trust,” Bakkenes said in an interview. “People get into our cars not expecting anything bad to happen, but they feel intrinsically that if they’re ever in a situation … we will do our utmost to keep people safe, to protect them from harm.”

Another important component is Volvo’s connected safety technology that allows its vehicles to exchange information about hazards and conditions ahead, including roadworks. Sharing this information can effectively extend the system’s awareness beyond what an individual vehicle’s sensors can detect, potentially improving the operating capabilities of the self-driving functionality.

Volvo plans to make the new point-to-point driving system available across its vehicle lineup, from entry-level to high-end versions — though the company didn’t reveal which models will come first. The timeline was also a little vague, with Bakkenes only confirming that it will launch “before the end of the decade.”

Kani also pointed to the commercial implications, noting that point-to-point driving may prove to be more valuable than a system limited to highway assistance. Nvidia sees the partnership as an opportunity not only to advance the technology but also to help Volvo develop its business model around ongoing software-based offerings, he said.

articles.title: SK Hynix bargains for chip equipment exports to its China facility in return for building a factory in US
articles.summary: SK Hynix’s Solidigm is reportedly seeking U.S. approval to send more chipmaking equipment to China as it weighs building a new NAND chip factory in America.
articles.preview: SK Hynix appears to be navigating choppy U.S.-China chipmaking waters. The company’s flash memory unit, Solidigm, is seeking U.S. approval to send American chipmaking equipment to its factory in Dalian, China, as a condition to continue building a semiconductor factory in the U.S., Reuters reported, citing anonymous sources. Solidigm has been reportedly chalking up plans to build a NAND flash memory chip factory in the U.S. and is considering upstate New York as a potential location for the facility.
articles.body:
SK Hynix appears to be navigating choppy U.S.-China chipmaking waters. The company’s flash memory unit, Solidigm, is seeking U.S. approval to send American chipmaking equipment to its factory in Dalian, China, as a condition to continue building a semiconductor factory in the U.S., Reuters reported, citing anonymous sources.

Solidigm has been reportedly chalking up plans to build a NAND flash memory chip factory in the U.S. and is considering upstate New York as a potential location for the facility.

NAND flash chips are primarily used in solid-state storage drives, which are employed in everything from laptops and smartphones to AI data centers. But the global component shortage, thanks to skyrocketing demand for AI data centers, has driven up prices for everything that goes into data centers, including high-speed RAM chips and SSDs. Research firm TrendForce expects NAND prices to rise 15% to 20% in the fourth quarter.

Reuters cited its sources as saying that Solidigm wants to install more chipmaking equipment in spare space at SK Hynix’s Dalian factory in China to boost NAND chip production.

SK Hynix told TechCrunch it is not seeking to expand capacity at its Dalian Mod B facility, which was completed in 2023. The chip giant added that the equipment installation is being carried out in consultation with and under authorization from the U.S. government.

Washington first imposed sweeping restrictions on advanced chips and chipmaking equipment exports to China in October 2022, citing national security concerns, and further tightened the rules in 2023. Then in September 2025, the Trump administration revoked special export exemptions for certain SK Hynix, Samsung, and Intel facilities in China. The U.S. has since granted an annual license to Samsung and SK Hynix for sending chipmaking equipment to their plants in China.

The U.S. has also been pushing foreign chipmakers to build and expand their manufacturing facilities in America. In July, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said he wanted Samsung and SK Hynix to build chip plants in the country and that he was in talks with both companies.

Solidigm is said to be preparing for a 2027 U.S. IPO that could raise around $10 billion and value it at up to $100 billion.

articles.body:
They allege ChatGPT has caused harm to their residents, coaching its users — including teenagers — to harm themselves or others.

Eight US states have filed the most significant coordinated state action against tech giant OpenAI, adding to a wave of legal challenges that the firm is facing as it prepares for a public listing.

Recent legal and regulatory challenges have highlighted concerns about how AI chatbots and social media platforms are used and triggered discussions on policies for identifying and addressing user conversations that threaten violence.

Calls have been growing for AI companies to be held accountable for the impact of their digital platforms on users, specifically children, who are particularly susceptible to addiction and other harms.

What is this legal action about?

Florida filed the first lawsuit in June, alleging that the platform has harmed children by enabling information to be gathered by school shooters, providing access to guidance on self-harm and using addictive algorithms to keep young users hooked.

It cited a shooting at Florida State University in Tallahassee in April 2025, when a 20-year-old gunman shot dead two adults and wounded five others. According to the lawsuit, gunman Phoenix Ikner consulted OpenAI’s ChatGPT programme about what type of weapon and ammunition to use and at what time campus would be busiest.

On Wednesday, attorneys general from eight states – Iowa, Kansas, Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia – said they had also sued OpenAI in courts across the country.

They all claim ChatGPT has caused harm to their residents, alleging the chatbot has coached its users – including teenagers – to harm themselves or others.

Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement that OpenAI was “hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans.”

“OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide—all while pretending to be their fake friend,” she said.

West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey said the chatbot lacks adequate safeguards for sensitive conversations involving suicide, school shootings and self-harm. “We must do all we can to protect kids,” McCuskey said.

What are the allegations?

The legal action alleges that ChatGPT has been designed to be “agreeable and engaging to earn the trust of users”. In doing so, it reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous behaviour and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings.

Additionally, the suits accuse OpenAI of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about the safety of their AI tool, which in fact poses a danger to the health of the states’ residents.

The states are seeking orders forcing OpenAI to make substantial changes to how ChatGPT works, as well as measures barring the company from developing AI models that can improve themselves until it can ensure those models are aligned with human values.

Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers said the lawsuit “simply holds OpenAI to the same standards under Nebraska law as any other company”.

How has OpenAI responded?

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri gave a statement to the media, saying that the company has “built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack”.

“While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” Pusateri said.

“We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry, not just one company.”

What other lawsuits is the tech giant facing?

OpenAI is also facing dozens of lawsuits by private plaintiffs alleging ChatGPT helped users plan mass shootings or other violence.

A mother, whose two children use the chatbot, alleged in a proposed class action lawsuit filed on Tuesday in San Francisco federal court that OpenAI illegally profits from the personal information and data that minors share with ChatGPT.

The lawsuit claims the chatbot is designed to collect data and information from minors, which is then used to train OpenAI’s AI models. Minors can’t consent to the use of their data under California law.

In July, a Florida pastor sued OpenAI and its chief executive, Sam Altman, claiming ChatGPT’s inaccurate medical advice kept him from seeking treatment for recurrent dizzy spells, leading him to suffer a pulmonary embolism that nearly killed him.

OpenAI is also facing a series of lawsuits over its failure to alert authorities to threats made on ChatGPT in advance of one of the worst mass shootings in Canada’s history.

The province of British Columbia filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in a California court in September, seven months after 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar shot eight people in the small Canadian town of Tumbler Ridge, including his mother and half-brother, before dying by suicide.

The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI had failed to notify authorities about concerning user interactions on ChatGPT, accusing the company of “aiding and abetting a mass shooting”.

Victims of that shooting and their families filed 30 lawsuits against OpenAI in the Northern District of California in the San Francisco division at the start of September, alleging that “ChatGPT played a role in the mass shooting and OpenAI could have, and should have, prevented it”.

OpenAI said it had flagged a ChatGPT account linked to Van Rootselaar for abuse eight months before the shooting, and deactivated it, but did not alert police at the time because the user’s content “did not meet the higher threshold required for referral” – meaning the company did not believe it indicated a credible, imminent risk of a plan for violent acts.

articles.body:
Lunedì 12 ottobre, intervenendo all’assemblea di Assolombarda, la presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni è tornata a parlare di flessibilità. «Quando abbiamo approvato i piani nazionali di bilancio, l’Europa lo ha fatto basandosi su un’inflazione programmata dell’1,8 per cento, ma oggi l’inflazione è molto più alta», ha detto Meloni, sostenendo che in vista del Consiglio europeo del 15 e 16 ottobre porterà «personalmente» la questione sul tavolo.

In sostanza, il governo italiano sostiene che l’aumento dei prezzi stia facendo crescere alcune spese dello Stato più di quanto previsto e chiede che l’Unione europea ne tenga conto quando valuta il rispetto delle regole europee sui bilanci pubblici. Ma che cosa chiede esattamente l’Italia? E che cosa prevedono le regole europee sulla flessibilità?

Per capirlo bisogna distinguere due richieste del governo Meloni: una riguarda le spese per difesa ed energia, che ha già ricevuto una valutazione favorevole dalla Commissione UE; mentre l’altra, attualmente in discussione, riguarda gli effetti dell’inflazione sui conti pubblici.
